The service door swings shut with a hollow clang behind the cart, wheels squeaking like a creature in pain. The donor who just watched his bid dissolve shoves past me without a glance, his shoulder bone jarring into mine hard enough to bruise. I barely feel it. My pulse is a live wire hammering against the inside of my throat, the silver cufflinks biting into my wrists where I’ve clenched my fists so tight my nails bite crescent moons into my palms. The host hasn’t given ground yet, still blocking the microphone like a bulwark, his face a mask of professional regret. Quinn’s grip on my forearm hasn’t loosened; her red dress flashes under the chandeliers like a warning signal. “He’s circling the back tables,” she says, voice low and urgent, “telling anyone who’ll listen your piece is compromised. But he still wants the closing dance.” The words land, but they don’t stick. My mouth is full of copper, the taste of champagne and failure lingering on my tongue.

I twist free. The host’s eyes widen when I step directly into his space, planting myself between him and the mic like a dam holding back the tide. The cart with my framed design is already halfway to the door, wheels grinding across the parquet. I raise my voice before it can vanish entirely, naming the piece out loud, forcing every eye back onto me. The room hums with murmurs, the kind that sound like a swarm of locusts settling on fresh grain. The donor lingers, glaring, his hand still outstretched like he expects the universe to correct itself. His heel scuffs the floor behind me—two steps, then he stops. Waiting. Judging.

Quinn’s fingers tighten again. “Mara—”

I don’t look at her. Can’t. My gaze is locked on the space behind the host, where Dorian’s presence has already rearranged the room. The air shifts, the way it does when someone significant walks into a space that was already crowded but suddenly feels empty. I feel it before I see him—the tug of gravity toward his location, the way the noise of the room dulls into the background like a radio dial turning down. He moves with the quiet confidence of a man who owns every second of every room he enters, shoulders rolling under a suit cut so precisely it looks like it was grown, not tailored. The fabric catches the light just enough to reveal the faintest pinstripes, the kind that aren’t meant to be seen unless you’re close enough to matter.

His face is the kind that reads like a map of his moods—strong jawline shadowed under sharp cheekbones, eyes so dark they look almost black in this dim light, but with an undertone that glints copper when he turns slightly, like embers catching the wind. The gap between his front teeth flashes when he smiles, a detail that makes his laughter contagious even when he’s not laughing. He’s broad enough to fill the doorway, but he doesn’t take up space by strutting. He just is. Present. Impossible to ignore.

I don’t know how long he’s been there. Minutes could have passed, or seconds. The host is still blocking the mic, the donor is still glaring, Quinn’s grip is still bruising my arm. But Dorian’s gaze lands on me like a physical touch, the kind that makes your skin prickle even through layers of fabric. His expression doesn’t change—still guarded, still calculating—but his eyes trace the line of my throat before flicking back to meet mine. A beat of silence stretches between us, thick enough to choke on.

He doesn’t speak. Doesn’t need to. The weight of his attention is enough to make my breath stutter in my chest. The cufflinks bite deeper. I can feel the sweat gathering at the base of my spine, the kind that comes from being too aware of too many things at once—my pulse, his gaze, the way the room seems to tilt when he steps closer.

He’s close enough that I can see the faint scar through his left eyebrow, only visible when he looks down. It’s the kind of detail that should be unremarkable, but it’s not. It’s the kind of thing that makes you wonder about the story behind it, the kind of thing that makes you want to reach out and trace it with your fingers. My hand moves before I can stop it, fingers curling into the fabric of my skirt like I’m anchoring myself to the ground.

Dorian’s gaze follows the motion, then lifts to my face again. His expression is unreadable, but his thumb works the cufflink at his opposite wrist—slow, deliberate, like he’s winding something down. The gesture is unconscious, familiar. It’s the kind of thing that makes you want to know what he’s hiding, what he’s trying to control.

I realize the great-grandmother’s old tarot deck is still in my hand. Reassuringly solid. Present. One of the heavy gold cards slips out—Petition Fate is inscribed in it. If only it were that easy. I would wish myself a way out. No—a way in. If only…

The grand staircase draped in silk caught the light in long, pale folds that made every step upward feel like surrender. I turned toward it instead, the deck heavy against my palm, and the donor’s glare still burned between my shoulder blades. I needed out before the next wave of whispers found me.

Dorian’s voice cut across the space between us, low and even. “Running won’t change what they saw.”

My fingers tightened around the top card. The wish formed before I could stop it: *I wish someone would see the work the way it was meant to be seen.* The silk above me rippled once, as if a draft had passed, though the air in the ballroom stayed still. A ridiculous coincidence. Nothing more.

I kept moving, skirt twisting around my ankles, the tremor in my hands betraying every careful line of my posture. Lila’s red dress flashed at the edge of my vision, but she didn’t reach for me. She knew better than to try.

A letter slid across the polished table just ahead of my path—thick, cream stock with his precise handwriting angled across the front. Dorian didn’t chase. He simply placed it where I would have to see it or step over it.

“The buyer is still interested,” he said. “Read it or don’t. But don’t pretend the room didn’t just watch you leave the only person willing to salvage the night.”

My heel caught the edge of the lowest step. The silk above shivered again, and the card in my hand felt suddenly warm. I realized the deck was still in my hand. As I slide Petition Fate back in, I notice a flash of red in the otherwise gold stack. "Tempt Fate." Grandma never let me play with that one. The service door slams again before I’ve fully turned my back, the hollow clang swallowed by the gilded corridor. My pulse hasn’t settled since the donor’s shoulder slammed into mine—hard enough to bruise, impossible to ignore. I don’t look at Quinn’s red dress cutting a line under the chandeliers. I don’t look at the host’s regret, or the framed design vanishing toward the door. The silk trembles slightly; the vent above the landing pushes a narrow current across the fabric. I realize I’m still clutching the tarot card—Petition Fate—its gold edges warm against my palm. The weight of it anchors me, a reminder that I’m not drowning. Not yet. The card slips once in my grip, the heavy gold catching the light where my thumb shifts. A coincidence. Or a nudge.

Dorian’s presence registers before I see him, a shift in the pressure of the room. A draft from the vent flutters again, and I wonder if it’s the air conditioning or if someone just passed close enough to stir it. My heel clicks once against the floorboard. I don’t stop walking. The staircase looms larger with every step, the silk now a barrier between me and whatever waits above. The card in my hand feels heavier, the words on it suddenly irrelevant. The grand staircase draped in silk seems to pulse, the fabric lifting and settling with each footfall on the steps below.

A hand brushes my wrist—light, almost accidental. I jerk back before I can stop myself, the tarot card slipping between my fingers, the gold edges glinting as it falls. The silk on the staircase ripples, the motion too sharp to be natural. A drop of sweat slides from my hairline down the back of my neck. I don’t look at the card. I don’t look at the hand that touched me. The silk trembles again, the folds rearranging where the air moves through them. The hallway stretches longer than it should, the distance to the staircase pulling at each step.

The grand staircase draped in silk waits, silent and watching. The hallway feels narrower now, the walls pressing in just enough to make breathing harder. I take a step forward, then stop. The hallway feels colder now, the air thick with something unseen. I take the first step onto the silk, the fabric cool against my shoe. I take another step, then another, the fabric cool against my shoe.

My pulse hasn’t settled since the donor’s shoulder slammed into mine—hard enough to bruise, impossible to ignore. I flex my fingers once, testing the sting, but the pain is already retreating, dulled by the weight in my chest. I don’t look at the stained champagne on my tongue. I don’t look at Quinn’s red dress cutting a line under the chandeliers. I don’t look at the host’s regret, or the framed design vanishing toward the door. My gaze stays fixed ahead, on the staircase railing, hand-polished walnut under the chandeliers, the folds catching the light where a draft crosses them.

The silk trembles slightly; the vent above the landing pushes a narrow current across the fabric. I realize I’m still clutching the tarot card—Petition Fate—its gold edges warm against my palm. The weight of it anchors me, a reminder that I’m not drowning. Not yet. The card slips once in my grip, the heavy gold catching the light where my thumb shifts. A coincidence. Or a nudge.

Dorian’s presence registers before I see him, a shift in the pressure of the room. A draft from the vent flutters again, and I wonder if it’s the air conditioning or if someone just passed close enough to stir it. My heel clicks once against the floorboard. I don’t stop walking. The staircase looms larger with every step, the silk now a barrier between me and whatever waits above. The card in my hand feels heavier, the words on it suddenly irrelevant. The grand staircase draped in silk seems to pulse, the fabric lifting and settling with each footfall on the steps below.

A hand brushes my wrist—light, almost accidental. I jerk back before I can stop myself, the tarot card slipping between my fingers, the gold edges glinting as it falls. The silk on the staircase ripples, the motion too sharp to be natural. A drop of sweat slides from my hairline down the back of my neck. I don’t look at the card. I don’t look at the hand that touched me. The silk trembles again, the folds rearranging where the air moves through them. The hallway stretches longer than it should, the distance to the staircase pulling at each step.

I force my fingers to unclench, the tension leaving my shoulders in a rush. The silk on the staircase sags slightly where the current thins. My pulse steadies, but my skin still prickles where the hand touched me. The tarot card lies forgotten on the floor, gold against dark wood, the words on it obscured. The grand staircase draped in silk waits, silent and watching. The hallway feels narrower now, the walls pressing in just enough to make breathing harder. I take a step forward, then stop. The silk on the staircase ripples once more, the motion too deliberate to be air.

A voice cuts through the silence—I don’t recognize it, don’t care to. The words are lost in the sudden stillness, but the tone is unmistakable: urgent, insistent. The silk on the staircase flutters, the folds catching the light where the vent current crosses them. My thumbnail finds the seam of my cuff and worries at a loose thread. I force myself to take another step, then another. The staircase looms larger with every stride, the silk now a shroud between me and whatever waits above. The hallway stretches further than it should, the distance to the staircase pulling at each stride.

The silk trembles one last time, the motion too sharp to be natural. My breath catches, but I don’t stop. I don’t look back. The tarot card is still on the floor, gold against dark wood, the words on it hidden. The grand staircase draped in silk stands before me, silent and expectant. The hallway feels colder now, the air thick with something unseen. I take the first step onto the silk, the fabric cool against my shoe. The staircase creaks slightly under my weight, the sound too loud in the quiet.

I don’t look up. I don’t look back. The silk on the staircase ripples once more, the folds rearranging where the air moves through them. The hallway stretches behind me, the distance to the door pulling at each stride. The tarot card is still on the floor, gold against dark wood, the words on it lost. The grand staircase draped in silk waits, silent and watching. The air in the hallway feels charged, the silk on the staircase the only thing moving. I take another step, then another, the fabric cool against my shoe.

I kept moving, skirt twisting around my ankles, the tremor in my hands betraying every careful line of my posture. Lila’s red dress flashed at the edge of my vision, but she didn’t reach for me. She knew better than to try.

A letter slid across the polished table just ahead of my path—thick, cream stock with his precise handwriting angled across the front. Dorian didn’t chase. He simply placed it where I would have to see it or step over it.

“The buyer is still interested,” he said. “Read it or don’t. But don’t pretend the room didn’t just watch you leave the only person willing to salvage the night.”

My heel caught the edge of the lowest step. A faint creak came from the banister as my weight shifted, and the card in my hand felt suddenly warm. I realized the deck was still in my hand. As I slid Petition Fate back in, I noticed a flash of red in the otherwise gold stack. "Tempt Fate." Grandma never let me play with that one. A sword raised to a blood-red sky, lightning arcing down from the clouds—or maybe arcing up? Ow! Static shock reminded me I needed to pay attention to the present…

Dorian’s voice cut across the space between us, low and even. “Running won’t change what they saw.”

My fingers tightened around the top card. The wish formed before I could stop it: *I wish someone would see the work the way it was meant to be seen.* The silk above me rippled once, as if a draft had passed, though the air in the ballroom stayed still. A ridiculous coincidence. Nothing more.

I kept moving, skirt twisting around my ankles, the tremor in my hands betraying every careful line of my posture. Lila’s red dress flashed at the edge of my vision, but she didn’t reach for me. She knew better than to try.

A letter slid across the polished table just ahead of my path—thick, cream stock with his precise handwriting angled across the front. Dorian didn’t chase. He simply placed it where I would have to see it or step over it.

“The buyer is still interested,” he said. “Read it or don’t. But don’t pretend the room didn’t just watch you leave the only person willing to salvage the night.”

My heel caught the edge of the lowest step. A faint creak came from the banister as my weight shifted, and the card in my hand felt suddenly warm. I realized the deck was still in my hand. Grandma never let me play with that one. A sword raised to a blood-red sky, lightning arcing down from the clouds (or maybe arcing up?) Ow! Static shock reminds me I need to pay attention to the present…

I realize the deck is still in my hand. As I slide Petition Fate back in, I notice a flash of red in the otherwise gold stack. "Tempt Fate." Ow!
